strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video diffusion and presents a useful post-training alternative to training a linear-attention generator from scratch. On Wan1.3B, replacing selected attention layers yields a reported 1.43x speedup at the main setting, with 1.52–2.00x speedups for longer sequences and only small changes on the reported VBench metrics.

The combination of learnable per-layer mixing, a cardinality constraint, and a binarizing regularizer is simple and practically motivated. The target-count sweep exposes the quality–efficiency tradeoff, and the severe degradation without the regularizer provides evidence that progressive, near-binary conversion matters.

The objective ablations are informative: ADM substantially improves the reported quality over latent MSE and final-distribution matching, while avoiding the extra score model and roughly 4.4x training cost associated with the compared DMD variants.
The manuscript is generally readable, and it evaluates both generation quality and measured end-to-end latency on an H100 rather than relying only on theoretical complexity or FLOPs.
weaknesses: The central ADM derivation is insufficiently justified. Equation 11 takes an expectation over samples from the converted model's marginal q_t, but the implemented sample in Equation 12 is a single Euler update starting from a teacher-precollected state x_{t'}, which is not generally distributed as q_t. More importantly, a rectified-flow velocity model can be converted to the score of its prescribed Gaussian interpolation marginal when it is the corresponding conditional velocity; after arbitrary attention replacement and fine-tuning, the current network is not automatically the score of its own ODE-generated marginal q_t. Thus Equation 13 does not establish that the implemented gradient is the claimed KL gradient. The loss may still be effective as teacher–student velocity matching, but the paper's principal distribution-matching interpretation lacks technical support.

The selective-transfer equations are internally inconsistent. In Equation 8, r weights quadratic attention, so the number of linearized layers is N minus the number of r values rounded to one. Equation 9 instead constrains the sum of rounded r values to `target`, although the experiments define `target=16` as 16 of 30 layers being linearized. The paper also writes a ceiling operator while describing thresholding at 0.5; an actual ceiling maps every positive r to one. These are consequential specification errors because they affect the central selection algorithm and its reproducibility.

The empirical evidence is narrow for the breadth of the claims: all main experiments use one relatively small backbone, Wan1.3B, at one resolution and nominal five-second duration. Only eight selected VBench dimensions are reported rather than the complete standard evaluation, VBench-2.0 is summarized without uncertainty, and there is no human preference study or temporal-artifact evaluation despite flicker and jitter being a motivation. Differences from dense attention are often only a few tenths of a point, with no repeated-run variance or significance analysis to support the terms “lossless” and “far outperforms.”

The efficiency accounting is incomplete. There are no peak-memory, attention-kernel latency, FLOP, or training-plus-teacher-data-generation costs, even though the method requires 50K teacher input/output pairs and approximately 28 training hours on eight H100s. The headline 15.92x result additionally changes the sampler from 50 to four steps using DMD2, so most of that gain cannot be attributed specifically to linear attention; a four-step dense-attention DMD2 control is needed to isolate the contribution.

The evidence for automatic layer selection is confounded. The “Manual” baseline uses the same final layer indices but replaces them before training, whereas LINVIDEO uses progressive mixed branches. Their difference therefore demonstrates the benefit of progressive relaxation, not that the learned selector finds better layers. The heuristic comparison is also hard to assess because its grid-search details are deferred to an appendix that is absent from the submitted PDF.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript repeatedly refers to an appendix, but the provided document contains no appendix. Important details are therefore unavailable, including the prompt/condition source for synthetic trajectories, whether “50K pairs” means trajectories or individual timestep pairs, batch size, learning-rate values, alpha-annealing schedule, baseline sparsity/configurations, and several promised derivations and qualitative results. “Data-free” should also be qualified as original-training-data-free, since the procedure still depends on teacher-generated samples and unspecified text conditions.

Because 14 quadratic-attention layers remain in the main model, its asymptotic attention complexity is still O(n^2), even if the quadratic coefficient is reduced. The title's qualified “towards O(n)” is defensible, but broader statements suggesting that the resulting model itself has linear asymptotic attention complexity are not supported.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical problem: reducing the cost of pretrained video diffusion transformers without requiring full retraining or access to the original video corpus.

The combination of layer-wise attention conversion and intermediate-timestep distribution matching is potentially useful. On Wan-1.3B, replacing 16 of 30 attention layers reportedly preserves the selected VBench metrics while providing a measured 1.43x end-to-end speedup on one H100.

The experiments include comparisons with several sparse-attention baselines, target-layer-count sweeps, objective ablations, and latency measurements over different frame counts. The particularly poor results without the binarization regularizer clearly demonstrate that smooth conversion is important.
weaknesses: The ADM derivation rests on an insufficiently justified score estimate. The paper treats the velocity of the model currently being modified as the score of q_t, although q_t is defined through samples obtained by applying the student to teacher-trajectory states. During conversion, the student need not be an optimal flow-matching model for its own induced marginals, so its velocity cannot automatically provide the claimed score. Equation (13) is presented without the promised appendix derivation or an analysis of the approximation error. This affects the technical foundation of the main objective.

The layer-selection ablation is substantially confounded. “Manual” uses exactly the layers discovered by LINVIDEO but hard-replaces them before training, whereas LINVIDEO performs gradual mixed-attention conversion. Their large gap therefore supports progressive conversion, not learned layer selection. The comparison between Manual and Heuristic is circular as evidence for automatic selection because Manual inherits LINVIDEO’s selected indices. A comparison controlling the conversion schedule is needed to support the selection claim.

The selection formulation is internally inconsistent. The text describes thresholding at 0.5, but Equations (9) and the surrounding discussion use ceil(r), which equals one for every positive r in [0,1], rather than nearest-integer rounding. This changes the constraint and its STE gradient behavior and makes the stated method difficult to reproduce. Equation (8) also uses division by d where the preceding softmax-attention definition uses sqrt(d).

The empirical scope is too narrow for the broad claims: all main experiments use a single 1.3B model, one resolution, one duration, and one hardware platform. There is no evidence on another architecture or model scale, no memory measurement, no FLOP analysis, no repeated-run uncertainty, and no human evaluation of temporal artifacts. Only eight selected VBench dimensions are tabulated, while the VBench-2.0 results are compressed into a rounded radar plot.

Claims such as “lossless,” “far outperforms,” and “extensive experiments” overstate the evidence. On Table 1, many differences from FlashAttention2 and SVG2 are only a few tenths of a metric point and may be within evaluation variability, which is not reported. The 15.92x headline speedup additionally compares a 4-step distilled model with a 50-step baseline, so most of that gain cannot be attributed to linear attention.

Reproducibility is weak in the provided manuscript. It repeatedly defers the ADM derivation, prompt/data construction, heuristic search, hyperparameters, additional ablations, and qualitative results to an appendix that is not present. The source of the conditioning prompts used to create the 50K teacher pairs is unspecified, making the precise meaning of “data-free” unclear. Exact latency values are also shown only graphically.

Baseline coverage and attribution need more care. Potentially strong methods are excluded based on training cost or supported shapes, and the paper itself acknowledges that sparse baselines are evaluated outside the larger-model/high-resolution regimes where their acceleration is more pronounced. Moreover, DMD2 is incorrectly cited as reference [30], which is a person-reidentification paper; the apparent intended reference is [58]. Overall, the practical result is promising, but the unresolved technical justification, confounded core ablation, and limited evidence currently outweigh it.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video diffusion transformers: reducing quadratic attention cost without full retraining. Post-training conversion of a pretrained model is potentially much more accessible than training a linear-attention video generator from scratch.

LINVIDEO combines two technically sensible components: differentiable, target-constrained layer selection and distribution matching along the sampling trajectory. The latter is particularly useful because it exploits the current multi-step model as a score estimator, avoiding the additional score network used by conventional distribution-matching distillation.

The empirical results show a favorable tradeoff on Wan1.3B. Replacing 16 of 30 attention layers yields a reported 1.43x end-to-end speedup while approximately preserving the selected VBench metrics; longer-sequence experiments report 1.52-2.00x speedups. Combining the method with four-step DMD2 gives a much larger 15.92x acceleration with a moderate metric decrease.

The ablations support the main design choices. Learned progressive transfer substantially outperforms manual initialization followed by training and a heuristic selection rule; removing the gate regularizer causes a severe collapse; and ADM clearly outperforms direct output matching and conventional final-distribution matching under the reported setup.

The target-layer ablation exposes the quality-efficiency frontier rather than reporting only a favorable operating point. Results on both VBench and VBench-2.0, together with qualitative examples, provide multiple forms of evidence.

The paper is generally well organized, motivates the representation gap between softmax and linear attention clearly, and offers a practically useful contribution even though it does not claim state-of-the-art generation quality.
weaknesses: The principal evidence is limited to a single 1.3B backbone, one video resolution/duration regime, and apparently one training run per configuration. Consequently, the claims that the procedure applies broadly to pretrained video diffusion models and provides 'lossless' conversion are stronger than the evidence. Small differences from FlashAttention2 on VBench are not accompanied by uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or human evaluation.

There is a concrete inconsistency in the selective-transfer formulation. Since r=1 selects quadratic attention and r=0 selects linear attention, Eq. (9), which constrains sum ceil(r) to 'target,' counts retained quadratic layers, whereas the text and experiments define target as the number of replaced linear layers. For N=30 and target=16 these differ. The listed selected set contains 16 linearized layers, suggesting a correctable equation or description error, but the manuscript should resolve it.

ADM is presented as minimizing the KL divergence, but its practical score for q_t is only approximated by the model currently undergoing architectural conversion. The justification that this model remains a calibrated flow model because conversion is progressive is plausible but not rigorous. No direct diagnostic of score accuracy or trajectory-distribution alignment is provided, so the theoretical wording should acknowledge this approximation.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript. It repeatedly defers the prompt/data construction, gate schedule, alpha ablation, heuristic search, temporal-artifact evidence, and other implementation details to an Appendix, but no appendix is included. In particular, 'data-free' generation still requires conditioning prompts, whose source and distribution are not specified, and '50K input-output pairs' is ambiguous about the number of independent trajectories.

The evaluation uses only eight selected VBench dimensions rather than the complete benchmark, while several reported gains over dense attention are very small. VBench-2.0 results are presented mainly as a radar plot and total score, making exact per-dimension comparison difficult. A broader metric suite and user study would better substantiate preservation of temporal quality and prompt fidelity.

The latency comparison lacks enough implementation detail to fully assess fairness, including baseline sparsity settings, compilation and precision settings, memory usage, warm-up/repetition protocol, and whether every implementation is comparably optimized. Training cost is also not quantified clearly enough to determine the deployment break-even point.

Several presentation errors should be corrected: Eq. (8) appears to scale attention logits by d rather than sqrt(d), inconsistent with the preliminaries; DMD2 is cited as reference [30] in the implementation section even though [30] is an unrelated person-reidentification paper; and claims such as 'far outperforms' and 'lossless' overstate mostly modest benchmark differences. These are mostly correctable, but the equation inconsistencies currently create avoidable uncertainty about the implementation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video diffusion models: reducing attention cost without full retraining. Selectively replacing attention layers is well motivated by the demonstrated large variation in layer replaceability.

The combination of learnable layer selection, progressive mixed-attention transfer, and anytime distribution matching is technically interesting and more original than simply applying an existing linear-attention module.

Experiments cover two substantially different model scales, Wan 1.3B and 14B, at 480p and 720p. The reported 1.43–1.71x end-to-end acceleration with relatively stable VBench/VBench-2.0 scores is practically meaningful, even though it is not an asymptotically linear model.

The ablations are useful: they examine the number of replaced layers, hard versus progressive transfer, the regularizer and its hyperparameters, alternative objectives, and direct joint linearization/few-step distillation. The 14B result also provides evidence that the approach is not confined to a small model.

The manuscript is generally clear, and it reports relevant training resources, sample counts, batch sizes, layer indices for the 1.3B ablation, and fixed-hardware latency. The qualitative examples are consistent with the quantitative conclusion that much of the teacher's appearance quality is retained.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification of selective transfer is internally inconsistent. The paper states that r=1 selects quadratic attention, yet Eq. (9) constrains the sum of rounded r values to `target`, while `target` is repeatedly defined as the number of layers replaced by linear attention. For N=30 and target=16, the reported model has 16 linear layers and therefore 14 quadratic layers, contradicting Eq. (9). Moreover, the ceiling notation used in Eqs. (9)–(10) is incompatible with the stated threshold-at-0.5 rounding operation. This is more than a cosmetic notation issue because it prevents faithful implementation of a central component.

The justification of ADM is incomplete. q_t is defined through a one-step transformation of teacher-trajectory samples, but the paper treats the velocity output of the currently modified model as the exact score of q_t. A multi-step diffusion parameterization can produce a score estimate, but it is not shown that this estimate equals the score of the particular implicit distribution q_t during transfer. Thus Eqs. (12)–(13) should be presented as an approximation with its assumptions or supported by additional analysis; the empirical comparison to a learned score approximator does not establish the claimed identity.

The strongest quality claims rely almost entirely on automatic benchmark scores. Many differences from the dense teacher are only a few tenths of a point, but no uncertainty estimates, repeated-seed variation, or human preference study are reported. Still-frame grids also cannot substantiate temporal smoothness or the claimed absence of flicker. Consequently, claims such as “lossless” and “without compromising performance” are stronger than the evidence supports.

The efficiency characterization is narrow. Latency is measured at one video duration and sequence length, without peak-memory measurements, FLOPs, attention-specific timing, or scaling curves. Because 14/30 and 18/40 quadratic-attention layers remain, the complete models still have O(n^2) asymptotic attention cost; the work moves toward, rather than achieves, O(n) video generation.

Baseline coverage and comparability are limited. Some close methods are excluded because of hardware, shape, or training-resource constraints, and the sparse baselines appear to be selectively reimplemented without all auxiliary optimizations. These choices may be reasonable, but they make the conclusion that LINVIDEO broadly outperforms prior efficient-attention approaches less secure.

The “data-free” terminology is potentially misleading: training uses 50,000 teacher-generated trajectory pairs conditioned on prompts from OpenVid. The method avoids original videos, but it still requires external text data, extensive teacher sampling, storage, and substantial H100 compute. These costs are not included in the efficiency comparison.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: exact sampling schedules, classifier-free guidance details during data collection and training, DMD2 settings, linear-attention kernel implementation, 14B selected-layer indices, and variance across training runs are not reported. The absence of a stated code/model release further increases the burden of reproducing the reported latency and quality.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video diffusion and demonstrates meaningful end-to-end acceleration: 1.43x on Wan-1.3B and 1.71x on Wan-14B, with substantially larger gains after four-step distillation.

Selective layer conversion is sensible and empirically well motivated. The target-layer sweep and comparisons against manual and heuristic selection support the claim that attention layers differ substantially in replaceability.

The evaluation covers two model scales, two versions of VBench, fixed-resolution latency on an H100, qualitative examples, and ablations of the selection regularizer, training objective, and linearized-layer budget.

Reusing teacher trajectories avoids dependence on the original video training set. The paper also reports many useful implementation details, including sample counts, hardware, optimization settings, batch sizes, and evaluation sampling.
weaknesses: The theoretical interpretation of ADM is insufficiently justified. The stated q_t is induced by taking a student step from a teacher-generated x_{t'}, but the student velocity is then treated as an estimator of the score of that q_t. A modified velocity network is not generally the score/velocity field of this teacher-conditioned pushforward distribution. Thus Equations 11-13 do not clearly establish that the implemented update is the gradient of the claimed KL divergence. The paper offers an empirical rationale but not the assumptions or stop-gradient details needed to make this central contribution technically convincing.

The evidence for 'preserving generation quality' or 'lossless acceleration' relies almost entirely on automatic metrics. Several reported differences are very small, yet there are no confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, or human preference results. Frame strips cannot adequately assess motion, flicker, or temporal coherence, which are particularly relevant when modifying video attention.

All principal experiments use two sizes of the same Wan architecture. This demonstrates scaling within one family but does not establish that the layer-selection procedure or ADM generalizes across video-diffusion architectures, despite the framework-level presentation.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete relative to the central O(n) claim. Results are reported at only one sequence length per model, without empirical scaling curves, peak-memory measurements, FLOPs, or a breakdown separating attention savings from the remaining pipeline. The moderate 1.43-1.71x end-to-end gains therefore do not demonstrate the claimed asymptotic advantage in practice.

The baseline comparison is selective. The most directly related concurrent linear-attention post-training method, SLA, is omitted because its available kernel targets different hardware, while other methods are excluded for resource or shape constraints. These may be practical obstacles, but the resulting experiments mainly compare against sparse-attention methods and do not firmly establish the advantage over alternative linearization approaches.

The 'data-free' terminology is overstated: training uses prompts sourced from OpenVid and 50,000 teacher-generated input/output pairs. The method avoids original training videos, which is valuable, but it still requires external prompts, substantial teacher inference, and up to 32 H100 GPUs; the cost of constructing the synthetic set and the full 14B training cost are not reported.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing operational details for the attention kernels and baseline configurations, the exact 14B layer selection, and the ADM/DMD2 implementation. These omissions matter because latency and the proposed score-matching update are sensitive to implementation choices.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video diffusion transformers: reducing quadratic-attention cost without full pretraining. Selectively converting layers is a useful middle ground between dense and fully linear architectures.

The combination of learnable layer selection and progressive mixed-attention transfer is technically sensible. Experiments support the central observation that layers differ substantially in replaceability, and the target-layer and regularization ablations clarify the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff.

The empirical results are strong: LINVIDEO is evaluated on both Wan-1.3B and Wan-14B, at 480p and 720p, and achieves 1.43–1.71x end-to-end speedups while remaining close to the dense models on VBench and VBench-2.0. The gains over several sparse-attention baselines are practically meaningful even without a specialized linear-attention kernel.

The ADM objective is accompanied by comparisons against output matching, conventional distribution matching, and a separately trained score estimator. These ablations show substantial quality gains and roughly 4.4x lower training time than objectives requiring an auxiliary model.

The paper is generally clear and includes useful implementation information, qualitative comparisons, tradeoff studies, and experiments showing that linearization followed by DMD2 distillation can provide much larger overall acceleration.
weaknesses: The derivation of ADM does not fully justify its claimed KL gradient. The samples defining q_t are obtained by taking a student Euler step from teacher-trajectory states, so q_t is not obviously the marginal distribution induced by the current student flow. Consequently, the current model's velocity evaluated at the resulting sample is not necessarily the score of q_t required by Eq. (12). The score–velocity identity applies when the velocity and marginal path are mutually consistent; that condition is not established here. The empirical objective may still be effective, but its interpretation as exact distribution matching is insufficiently supported.

There is an internal inconsistency in the layer-count constraint. Since r=1 selects quadratic attention and r=0 selects linear attention, Eq. (9), (sum ceil(r)-target)^2, constrains the number of retained quadratic layers. The text and experiments instead define target as the number replaced by linear attention, with larger target producing lower latency. The stated loss would need N-target or a sum over 1-ceil(r). This may be a correctable equation error, but it directly affects reproducibility.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on automatic VBench scores, without human preference evaluation, uncertainty estimates, or results across multiple training seeds. Several reported differences from the dense model are small enough that their significance cannot be assessed, while qualitative figures contain only a few sequences and cannot expose broader temporal failure modes.

The claimed O(n) advantage is not characterized as sequence length changes. All principal latency measurements use one fixed video shape per backbone, and the paper reports neither memory usage nor an attention-only latency breakdown. Scaling curves would better establish when the asymptotic advantage translates into practical gains.

The description of the training objective omits consequential details such as how adjacent timesteps are sampled, whether score terms are stop-gradient targets, and how losses are normalized or weighted over timesteps. The method also requires 50K teacher trajectory pairs generated from OpenVid prompts, so 'data-free' should be qualified as video-data-free rather than suggesting that no external data or substantial teacher generation is needed.

The closest post-training mixed linear-attention method, SLA, is excluded because its optimized kernel targets different hardware. That explains why a latency comparison is difficult, but quality, replacement-rate, or kernel-independent comparisons would still improve the evidence for relative novelty and performance. The 15.9–20.9x headline speedups should also be interpreted cautiously because most of those gains come from the added DMD2 reduction from 50 to 4 sampling steps rather than from LINVIDEO itself.
